newsitem.title: GERMANY: Pro-genetic campaign aims to calm fears in Germany.
newsitem.headline: Pro-genetic campaign aims to calm fears in Germany.

text.p: Food containing genetically-modified organisms (GMOs) is no more risky to human health than other processed food products, experts said on behalf of German food institute BLL on Tuesday.

At a presentation by BLL officials and three academics, BLL officials said the organisation wanted a speedy implementation of rules setting out pan-European labelling practices for GMO-derived products to give consumers choices.
The speakers were starting a multi-city tour within Germany aimed at appeasing consumer fears over the new food products.
Opponents led by environmental organisation Greenpeace say too little is known about GMOs and that more time should be allowed to assess their possible effect on human health and the environment.

"Genetic technology will help improve the quality of food products, because we get to know more about them and can check their safety," said Klaus-Dieter Jany, head of the national food research institute in Karlsruhe.
He added the EU novel foods regulation, due to come into effect on May 15, would offer informative and clear labelling.

According to these rules, if there were traces of GMOs in the DNA of a product, it needed to be labelled but labelling was unnecessary where the products had changed to a degree making them identical with conventional ones, he said.
Labelling would also be a mandatory if certain foods were found to be causing allergies or if their make-up disqualified them for consumption by certain ethnic or religious groups.
BLL's managing director Matthias Horst said the main challenge was to agree identical testing procedures and labelling styles across Europe.
This would take additional time far beyond mid-May.
BLL was supporting retroactive rules on the labelling of products derived from genetically-altered soybeans and maize although they technically did not fall under novel foods.
Both commodities were approved for marketing in the EU last year, before the novel food law was drawn up.
Beda Stadler, a professor at Bern university, said genetic crop modification was highly unlikely to create new allergy risks and at the same time provided new ways of reducing existing risks.
BLL provides legal and scientific assistance to 300 companies in food production, trade and related services.
